questions.explanation: `std::remove` is an algorithm, so it only sees iterators and **cannot** change the container's size. It moves the kept elements to the front (`1 3 5 ? ?`) and returns the new logical end. You still need `v.erase(new_end, v.end())`. This is the erase-remove idiom.
`reserve` allocates raw storage only. It constructs nothing and leaves `size()` at 0. `c[5]` would be UB. `resize(100)` would construct 100 value-initialised points and set size to 100.

options: `erase` invalidates `it`, and the loop also skips the element after each erased one
`erase` is O(1), so it's just slow
questions.explanation: After `erase(it)`, `it` is invalidated, and incrementing it is UB. Even the 'fixed' version `it = cloud.erase(it);` followed by `++it` skips an element and is O(n²) overall, because each erase shifts the tail. Use `cloud.erase(std::remove_if(...), cloud.end())`, which is one O(n) pass.

The size is at capacity, so `push_back` reallocates: it allocates a new buffer, moves the elements over and frees the old one. Every pointer, reference and iterator now dangles. An **index** is just a number and stays meaningful. That's why SLAM maps often refer to landmarks by index or id.

Capacity grows geometrically (doubling in libstdc++): 1, 2, 4, …, 2^20, which is about 20 reallocations. Total copying stays O(n), so `push_back` is *amortised* O(1). Calling `reserve(1000000)` first cuts this to one allocation.

`clear()` destroys the elements but keeps the buffer. That's ideal for a per-scan scratch vector you reuse every frame: no malloc in the loop. To actually free the memory, use `shrink_to_fit()` (a non-binding request) or `std::vector<Point3>().swap(v)`.

questions.prompt: Which is the cheapest way to remove element `i` from a `std::vector<Point3>` when **order does not matter**?
options: Copy all other elements into a new vector
questions.explanation: Swap-and-pop is O(1). `erase` in the middle shifts the whole tail, which is O(n). This is the standard trick for unordered landmark or particle sets.

options: Compile error: `vector<bool>` returns a proxy object, not `bool&`
questions.explanation: `std::vector<bool>` is a bit-packed specialisation. `operator[]` returns a `std::vector<bool>::reference` proxy, so there's no real `bool` to bind to. It's also slow, and not thread-safe for writes to neighbouring bits. Robotics code often uses `std::vector<uint8_t>` for masks instead.
